content: Children under the age of five contribute significantly to the burden of chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infections in adults. The prevalence of HBV infection in this age group, determined by the presence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), serves as a surrogate indicator for the cumulative incidence of chronic HBV infection. To monitor and evaluate viral hepatitis programs effectively, data systems should ideally include surveillance of acute hepatitis, among other components. In the absence of established data systems, rapid data extraction methods can be employed during the initial assessment phase. Monitoring the cascade of testing and treatment is essential for improving patient management and identifying gaps in care delivery. The most effective approach to monitoring national HBV and hepatitis C virus (HCV) programs involves integrating these services into a broader health management information system, ensuring coordination and governance at the national level. Databases of individuals with chronic infections can provide longitudinal data based on individual records, but managing such databases is resource-intensive. Leveraging existing electronic reporting systems, medical records, and health records can facilitate monitoring the care cascade from individual patient management at the facility level to aggregate reporting at the central level. However, simpler methods using aggregated data from healthcare facilities can also estimate core indicators of testing and treatment, particularly in the early stages of program implementation. Aggregated data management is less labor-intensive and suitable for programs in the initial scale-up phase. Patient management tools, such as template cards, can be used in paper or electronic formats to document care practices. A subset of variables from these records can be entered into a case surveillance database, which tracks patients from diagnosis to treatment and outcomes, such as viral suppression or cure. These databases allow healthcare providers to manage data on patient characteristics, diagnosis, treatment, and monitoring while ensuring data confidentiality and avoiding duplication. They can also track individuals as part of an epidemiological cohort across the care cascade and between facilities. However, interoperability issues may arise when different health systems within a country use varying databases. Automated data analysis systems can aggregate individual data and calculate core indicators on diagnosis, treatment, and effectiveness, compiling data from different systems. Aggregated data on the care cascade can then be reported at the national level and ultimately to the World Health Organization (WHO) through the Global Reporting System on Hepatitis. This system uses a standardized application, such as the District Health Information System 2 (DHIS2), to facilitate data reporting. Strategic information is critical at all stages of a hepatitis program, including initial assessment, planning, implementation, and evaluation. During the initial assessment, baseline estimates of HBV and HCV prevalence are essential for setting priorities. Data extraction along core indicators provides an overview of the baseline situation, while national policies and plans document the level of commitment. The planning stage involves estimating the population requiring treatment to allocate resources effectively. Cost-effectiveness analyses can support the inclusion of interventions in national health benefit packages as part of Universal Health Coverage. At the implementation stage, countries must use domestically generated data to identify gaps in service coverage and quality systematically. Progress can also be reported internationally. During the final evaluation, the full set of core indicators can document the program's impact on incidence and mortality. Mathematical modeling can complement empirical data collection by estimating HBV and HCV prevalence, incidence, and mortality, as well as analyzing the cost and impact of various service coverage options. These models can guide national elimination plans and provide insights into the cost-effectiveness of interventions. In conclusion, the elimination of viral hepatitis requires the implementation of core interventions coordinated across health programs and services. Strategic information must be consolidated within the health information system to provide a comprehensive picture that guides elimination efforts at all program stages. While the described information system may seem ambitious, countries can start with simple elements and build upon them within their national health information systems. WHO is available to provide technical assistance as needed.
